elements.quote: This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of ER behavioral observation and physiological measures of children and adolescents, including their theoretical embedding and psychometric properties.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of ER behavioral observation and physiological measures of children and adolescents, including their theoretical embedding and psychometric properties.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit main objective of providing an overview of ER measures, including theoretical embedding and psychometric properties.

elements.quote: We included empirical studies assessing ER as an outcome variable in children and adolescents aged 0-15 years using at least one behavioral or physiological ER measure. Studies on secondary literature were excluded.
elements.reason: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are explicitly stated.

elements.quote: Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature search in PubMed, PsycINFO, Psyndex plus, and Web of Science without language restrictions.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies information sources (databases) but does not provide when each source was last searched.
The retrieved abstract text does not describe the methods used to assess risk of bias in included studies.

elements.quote: Measurement types, theoretical grounding, and psychometric properties (reliability, validity, objectivity) were extracted and compared across age groups using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the basic approach to comparing/extracting and using descriptive statistics/chi-square tests, but it does not clearly specify the full synthesis methods (e.g., overall synthesis approach for outcomes).

elements.quote: A total of 516 studies met inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies. (Participants and study characteristics are not explicitly quantified beyond general findings.)

elements.quote: Only 5% reported validity evidence, 62% reliability, and 20% objectivity. Few studies referenced an ER definition or empirically tested an ER model. LAB-TAB and Delay of Gratification tasks were the most common behavioral observation measures, whereas RSA and EEG dominated physiological measures. Behavioral observation was more frequently used in younger children, whereas physiological measures were more common in older children ( p < .001; V = .37). Most studies focused on the regulation of negative emotions (91%), and 90% relied on a single ER measure.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes/metrics, including proportions and comparative findings.
No meta-analysis is described in the retrieved abstract evidence, so the conditional requirement (summary estimate and confidence/credible interval) does not apply based on the provided text.

elements.quote: Behavioral observation was more frequently used in younger children, whereas physiological measures were more common in older children ( p < .001; V = .37).
elements.reason: The abstract indicates the direction of effect across compared groups (younger children favored behavioral observation; older children favored physiological measures).

elements.quote: Conclusion ER measurement in children and adolescents is characterized by limited psychometric reporting and insufficient theoretical integration.
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes limitations of the evidence in terms of limited psychometric reporting and insufficient theoretical integration.

elements.quote: This review provides an overview of available methods and their psychometric properties, facilitating the selection of appropriate measures for future research. Greater emphasis on validity... will be essential to improve comparability across studies and enhance the cumulative value of research on ER across developmental stages.
elements.reason: The abstract provides interpretation and implications for future research (selection of measures; emphasis on validity to improve comparability/cumulative value).
No primary funding source is reported in the retrieved abstract evidence.
No register name and registration number are reported in the retrieved abstract evidence.

elements.quote: A considerable proportion of studies (39%) did not report any psychometric information, meaning that the meta-analytic results were necessarily based on a subset of studies.... Taken together, the strong emphasis on reliability, combined with limited reporting of validity and substantial non-reporting overall, highlights a systematic imbalance in current practices.
elements.reason: The review describes the current state of knowledge as well as key uncertainties/gaps in psychometric reporting (e.g., non-reporting, limited validity evidence, reliance on reliability), which contextualizes the rationale.

elements.quote: Valid and reliable ER measures are needed to develop models for mental health promotion and treatment.
elements.reason: The abstract explains the importance/need for the review by stating why valid and reliable measurement is necessary for developing models for mental health promotion and treatment.
The retrieved evidence does not report whether similar systematic reviews exist or explain the need for a new/current review based on prior reviews (e.g., updates/replications with citations).

This criterion concerns intervention effects and mechanisms of action, but the retrieved evidence provided is about measurement/psychometric properties of emotion regulation measures rather than interventions.
This criterion is for complex interventions/delivery contexts requiring a logic model; the retrieved evidence does not indicate that the review is evaluating intervention delivery contexts.

elements.quote: Objectives |        2 | Provide an explicit statement of the main objective(s) or question(s) the review addresses. | yes
elements.reason: The checklist table indicates the objective/question is reported as “yes”, but the retrieved evidence does not provide the actual objective(s) or question(s) statement.
No retrieved evidence states planned comparisons using PICO (or an appropriate variant) for intervention effects.

elements.quote: Studies were included according to the PICOS criteria [177]. Eligible studies included participants from birth to 15 years and 11 months. Studies were required to use at least one ER measurement and report ER as an outcome variable. Both studies with and without group comparisons were eligible.
elements.reason: The evidence specifies key PICOS components for eligibility (participants’ age range; requirement for ER measurement and reporting ER as an outcome; inclusion of studies with/without group comparisons). However, it does not explicitly specify eligible study settings or follow-up requirements.

elements.quote: No language restrictions were applied; studies in all languages were included.
elements.reason: The evidence specifies the language criterion (no language restrictions). It does not report dissemination year limits or explicitly state publication/report status criteria.
The evidence does not describe a distinction between exclusions due to outcomes not being measured versus exclusions due to outcome results not being reported.
The evidence does not specify the groups used in each synthesis or how those groups relate to comparisons defined in the review objectives.

elements.quote: We initially preregistered an age range of 0 to 18 years. However, this age range was reduced to 0 to 15 years and 11 months due to the large number of eligible records identified.
elements.reason: The evidence provides a rationale for a notable restriction/change to study eligibility (reducing the preregistered age range due to the large number of eligible records).

elements.quote: The search was updated continuously until 13.09.2024.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the last search/update date (13.09.2024).

elements.quote: We used topic-specific databases PubMed (including MEDLINE; Ovid), PsycINFO (including PsycArticles; EBSCOhost), Psyndex plus (EBSCOhost) and Web of Science (Thomson Reuters, Clarivate Analytics) for adjoining disciplines.
elements.reason: Database names/platforms are reported, but coverage dates for each database are not provided in the retrieved evidence.
No study registers/regulatory databases/online repositories searched are described in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence names Google Scholar as excluded, but does not report any searched website/search engine with its name and URL.
While the authors state that authors were contacted, no organisations or manufacturers contacted are named in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: For studies with unavailable full-texts, authors were contacted or articles purchased.
elements.reason: The types of individuals contacted are partially described as 'authors', but no further detail is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Additionally, manual reference checks and citation tracking in the Social Science Citation Index were conducted.
elements.reason: The manuscript indicates manual reference checks (i.e., references were examined), but it does not specify the types of reference lists (e.g., bibliographies of included studies, specific collections) beyond that.

elements.quote: Additionally, manual reference checks and citation tracking in the Social Science Citation Index were conducted.
elements.reason: It reports the citation index/platform (Social Science Citation Index) but does not provide the seed reports or the search date for the citation tracking.
No journals or conference proceedings consulted (with dates covered and search methods) are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The search strategy was piloted in PubMed and adapted for each database (search strategy for PubMed, Appendix, File 3).
elements.reason: The manuscript states the search strategy was adapted for each database and points to Appendix File 3, but the retrieved evidence does not include the complete, full search strategies as actually run for every source.

elements.quote: No publication date limits were applied.
elements.reason: A specific limit (no publication date limits) is reported, but the retrieved evidence does not describe all search limits and how they were justified with reference to eligibility criteria.
The retrieved evidence does not cite published search approaches/filters or describe any adaptations to published filters beyond noting a previously pre-registered strategy was contrasted.

elements.quote: After screening 2977 articles, the artificial intelligence 'Rayyan' was used for further screening.
elements.reason: Rayyan is described for abstract screening, not for NLP/text-analysis tools used to identify or refine search terms; thus this criterion for search-term refinement tools does not apply based on the retrieved evidence.
No tools for translating search strings between sources are specified in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not report any validation of the search strategy or validation process/studies.
The retrieved evidence does not describe any peer review of the search strategy or use of PRESS (or similar).
The retrieved evidence does not explain a final conceptual structure and explorations used to develop the search when not based on PICO.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently screened by two authors (MB, RD) and two advanced graduate students. Each record was screened by at least one of the two authors. Discrepancies (29%) were resolved through discussion and consensus. All potentially eligible articles were independently assessed in full text by three authors (MB, RD, FS) and two advanced graduate students.
elements.reason: Reports the number/type of reviewers at title/abstract screening and full-text assessment, but does not explicitly report how many reviewers screened each record and each report retrieved at every stage (e.g., exact counts per stage/record).

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently screened by two authors (MB, RD) and two advanced graduate students.
elements.reason: States that screening of titles/abstracts was performed independently.

elements.quote: Discrepancies (29%) were resolved through discussion and consensus. ... Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Any discrepancies in ratings were discussed until consensus was reached.
elements.reason: Describes how disagreements/discrepancies were resolved (discussion and consensus; discussed until consensus).
No description is provided of processes to obtain/confirm eligibility information from study investigators.
No methods are reported for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.

elements.quote: After screening 2977 articles, the artificial intelligence 'Rayyan' was used for further screening. Rayyan has been proved as a reliable tool for abstract sreening [38, 214, 246].
elements.reason: Describes integration of an automation tool (Rayyan) into the selection process after an initial screening step.
No identification by version/reference of externally derived classifiers, nor reporting of records removed before screening in relation to such classifiers.
No internally derived classifier information (use/training/validation) is reported.
No machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules are described.
No crowdsourcing platform or integration into selection is described.
No description of previously screened datasets used to eliminate records (and how they were derived) is provided.
The evidence describes author numbers for screening/assessment, but does not report how many reviewers collected data from each report.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently screened by two authors (MB, RD) and two advanced graduate students.
elements.reason: Independence is described for screening, but independence for data collection/data extraction (the core focus of this item) is not clearly reported.

elements.quote: Discrepancies (29%) were resolved through discussion and consensus. Disagreements were resolved by consensus.
elements.reason: Processes for resolving disagreements between data collectors are explicitly described (discussion and consensus).
No processes are described for obtaining or confirming data from study investigators.
The evidence does not describe automation tools used for data collection, including use, training, or validation.
No methods for translating articles for data collection are reported.
The evidence does not specify software used to extract data from figures.
No decision rules are described for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies.

elements.quote: The primary outcome was the reporting of psychometric properties in behavioral and physiological ER measures.
elements.reason: A primary outcome is defined (reporting of psychometric properties in behavioral and physiological ER measures), but the evidence does not list and define all outcome domains for which data were sought.
No time frame of measurement for each outcome domain is specified in the retrieved evidence.
The evidence does not state whether all compatible results within each outcome domain were sought.
Because it is not reported whether not all compatible results were sought, the process used to select results (when applicable) is not described in the retrieved evidence.
No changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance with rationales are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains with rationales are reported in the retrieved evidence.
The evidence does not report which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions and the rationale for prioritization.

elements.quote: Extracted data comprised study identification, study and measurement characteristics (study design, publication type), sample characteristics (age, gender, ethnicity, child/family characteristics), definition/model of ER, measurement of ER and psychometric properties of ER measurements (reliability, validity, objectivity).
elements.reason: The review states what data were extracted (e.g., sample characteristics, study/measurement characteristics, ER definition/model, measurement, and psychometric properties). However, it does not explicitly list and define all other variables for which data were sought (e.g., funding sources or other potential variables are not mentioned), so completeness and “define” requirement are not fully met.
No description of any assumptions made about missing or unclear study information is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: For data extraction, an a priori-developed tool was piloted on the first five articles.
elements.reason: A tool is mentioned and described (an a priori-developed tool piloted), but it is not cited or otherwise identified in the retrieved evidence, so the citation requirement is only partially satisfied.

elements.quote: The revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool [227] was applied to randomized controlled trials... For non-randomized and observational quantitative studies, the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) Quality Assessment Tool was used [232].
elements.reason: The specific risk-of-bias tools used (revised Cochrane RoB tool and EPHPP Quality Assessment Tool) are named.

elements.quote: In the EPHPP tool, domains are rated as strong, moderate, or weak and a global rating is assigned based on the number of weak domains.
elements.reason: The EPHPP domain rating approach is described (strong/moderate/weak) and that a global rating is based on weak domains, but the individual domains/components/items are not explicitly listed. RoB 2 domain details are only indirectly suggested elsewhere.

elements.quote: RoB 2 classifies studies as low risk, some concerns, or high risk, depending on the highest risk level across domains.
elements.reason: Rules for deriving overall risk judgments are reported for RoB 2 (based on highest risk across domains). Additionally, EPHPP global rating rules are described in the same passage.

elements.quote: Within the EPHPP rating scheme, we excluded the 'Study Design' section, as it was not applicable to non-RCT studies.
elements.reason: A specific adaptation to the EPHPP tool is explicitly described (excluding the 'Study Design' section).
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is described, nor any statement about development and public accessibility.

elements.quote: All potentially eligible articles were independently assessed in full text by three authors (MB, RD, FS) and two advanced graduate students... Risk of bias assessments were also conducted by the three authors (MB, RD, FS) and trained graduate students. Any discrepancies in ratings were discussed until consensus was reached.
elements.reason: The number of assessors and roles are described (three authors and trained graduate students) and consensus resolution is stated. However, it does not clearly specify whether risk-of-bias assessments themselves were performed independently (independence is stated for full-text assessment, not explicitly for risk-of-bias ratings).
The evidence does not describe processes to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators.
No automation tools used for risk-of-bias assessment (including training/validation) are reported.

elements.quote: Differences in reporting frequencies across psychometric properties were examined using Fisher's exact tests. The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The effect measure(s) used for the synthesis/presentation of outcomes described in this evidence (proportions of studies reporting psychometric properties using random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions; Fisher's exact tests for between-group differences) are specified, but no explicit mapping of effect measures to every outcome/outcome type is shown in the retrieved text.
The retrieved evidence does not report any thresholds or ranges used to interpret effect sizes (e.g., cutoffs for what constitutes a small/medium/large effect) or their rationale.
No methods for re-expressing synthesized results using another effect measure are described in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence provides the statistical approach used (e.g., logit-transformed proportions with Hartung-Knapp), but does not justify the choice of effect measure.

elements.quote: Studies were included according to the PICOS criteria [177]. Eligible studies included participants from birth to 15 years and 11 months. Studies were required to use at least one ER measurement and report ER as an outcome variable. Both studies with and without group comparisons were eligible. No language restrictions were applied; studies in all languages were included. We initially preregistered an age range of 0 to 18 years. However, this age range was reduced to 0 to 15 years and 11 months due to the large number of eligible records identified.
elements.reason: The review describes eligibility criteria for including studies (PICOS, participant age range, ER measurement/outcome, language, and age-range revision), but it does not describe the specific processes used to decide eligibility for each synthesis or the planned groups for each synthesis (e.g., tabulating study intervention characteristics and comparing against planned groups).

elements.quote: “T o facilitate comparison across studies, RoB 2 ratings were converted into a numerical format consistent with the EPHPP system (1 = low risk, 2 = some concerns, 3 = high risk).”
elements.reason: The review describes at least one data conversion step used in preparation for analysis (conversion of RoB 2 ratings into a numerical EPHPP-consistent format). However, the evidence provided does not describe other required preparation methods for presentation/synthesis such as handling missing summary statistics or additional data conversions.

elements.quote: Types of measures for ER based on behavioral observations and physiological measurements are described in the Supplementary Material (Tables 1a-1e and 2a-2e). For each study, the minimum age at which the ER measurement was applied was used; if no minimum age was reported, the mean age was applied. Based on these values, measures were organized into broader age groups (neonates, infants, toddlers, preschool, school-aged children and teens) according to the American Academic of Pediatrics [6].
elements.reason: The report describes the tabular structures used (Supplementary Material Tables 1a–1e and 2a–2e) and the data included/organized within them (e.g., age used per study and resulting age-group categories).

No description is provided of the graphical methods used to display results (e.g., what figures/plots are used and how they present study/synthesis results). A figure is referenced, but the graphical method is not described.

elements.quote: Based on these values, measures were organized into broader age groups (neonates, infants, toddlers, preschool, school-aged children and teens) according to the American Academic of Pediatrics [6]. These broader categories were further divided into narrower age groups of 12 months categories. Within these 12 months categories the measures are organized according to the examined emotions (frustration/anger/disappointment, fear, jealousy, empathy, joy and non-specific emotion/mixed emotions).
elements.reason: The basis for ordering/grouping the (tabulated) measures is explicitly reported (age grouping using minimum/mean age and organization by emotions within 12-month categories).
The rationale for using non-standard graphs is not reported in the available evidence.
No software package(s) or version numbers used for statistical synthesis are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The retrieved evidence indicates that a meta-analysis was performed; therefore an alternative synthesis method for cases where meta-analysis was not possible is not applicable.

elements.quote: The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The model is described (random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with Hartung-Knapp adjustment), but the rationale for choosing this model is not provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The statistical method used for the meta-analysis is explicitly reported (logit-transformed proportions; inverse-variance weighting; Hartung-Knapp adjustment).

elements.quote: Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q and the I 2 statistic.
elements.reason: Methods to identify/quantify statistical heterogeneity are explicitly reported (Cochran's Q and I²).
The retrieved evidence does not report the between-study variance estimator for the random-effects meta-analysis.
The retrieved evidence does not state how confidence intervals for the summary effect were calculated.
No additional random-effects implementation details are reported in the retrieved evidence beyond the brief description of the random-effects approach and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.

elements.quote: The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The retrieved evidence describes a (frequentist) random-effects meta-analysis and does not indicate that Bayesian meta-analysis was performed.
The retrieved evidence does not describe any methods to account for statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study.
The retrieved evidence does not identify planned syntheses that were judged impossible/inappropriate or provide reasons for not conducting them.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were conducted by age group and measurement type, with between-group differences evaluated using Q-tests.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports using subgroup analyses (age group, measurement type) and Q-tests to explore heterogeneity/between-group differences.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were conducted by age group and measurement type, with between-group differences evaluated using Q-tests.
elements.reason: Factors (age group, measurement type) are reported, but specific factor levels and any expected direction of effect modification are not provided in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not specify whether heterogeneity analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were conducted by age group and measurement type, with between-group differences evaluated using Q-tests.
elements.reason: Methods to compare subgroup effects are described (between-group differences evaluated using Q-tests).
No informal methods for exploring heterogeneity (when meta-analysis was unsuitable) are described in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not indicate whether any heterogeneity analyses were not pre-specified.

elements.quote:
Sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine the robustness of the findings across risk-of-bias ratings. These analyses were based on 288 studies, as 26 studies included both measurement types but only one studylevel risk-of-bias rating.
...
Results were consistent across risk-of-bias groups, with proportions of 70.8% for high risk (95% CI [65.2, 75.9], k = 17), 64.5% for low risk (95% CI [61.8, 67.1], k = 151), and 63.6% for moderate risk (95% CI [60.5, 66.6], k = 120). No significant between-group differences were observed, Q(2) = 5.81, p = 0.055, Cohen's h = 0.15.
...
Subgroup estimates were similar across risk levels: 24.8% for high risk (95% CI [21.2, 28.6], k = 17), 23.9% for low risk (95% CI [22.5, 25.3], k = 151), and 23.5% for moderate risk (95% CI [22.0, 24.9], k = 120). No significant subgroup differences were found, Q(2) = 0.52, p = 0.772, Cohen's h = 0.03.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that sensitivity analyses were performed to test robustness across risk-of-bias ratings and provides the results (proportions, k, CIs, heterogeneity and between-group tests) for reliability/validity/objectivity.

The retrieved evidence describes sensitivity analyses and their outcomes, but does not state whether any sensitivity analyses were not pre-specified or identify which analyses were/weren't pre-specified.

No methods are described for assessing risk of bias due to missing results in the synthesis (arising from reporting biases). The retrieved text describes risk-of-bias ratings and reasons for moderate/high ratings (e.g., selection of reported results, blinding, dropout) but does not state a specific method for assessing missing-result reporting bias.

elements.quote: For non-randomized and observational quantitative studies, the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) Quality Assessment Tool was used [232]. ... In the EPHPP tool, domains are rated as strong, moderate, or weak and a global rating is assigned based on the number of weak domains. RoB 2 classifies studies as low risk, some concerns, or high risk, depending on the highest risk level across domains.
elements.reason: The review reports using existing tools (RoB 2 and EPHPP) and specifies how domains are rated and how a global judgement is derived for EPHPP, and the basis for RoB 2 overall classification.

elements.quote: Within the EPHPP rating scheme, we excluded the 'Study Design' section, as it was not applicable to non-RCT studies. T o facilitate comparison across studies, RoB 2 ratings were converted into a numerical format consistent with the EPHPP system (1 = low risk, 2 = some concerns, 3 = high risk).
elements.reason: Adaptations to an existing tool(s) are explicitly reported: excluding the 'Study Design' section for non-RCTs and converting RoB 2 ratings to a numerical format consistent with EPHPP.
There is no description of any newly developed reporting-bias tool or its public accessibility in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently screened by two authors (MB, RD) and two advanced graduate students. Each record was screened by at least one of the two authors. elements.quote:
Across measurement types, most moderate ratings in the RoB 2 scheme were due to the domain "Selection of the reported results", with 43% of studies ( n = 13) lacking pre-registration.

elements.quote: However, this review has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, the restricted age range, which was necessary for feasibility, limits the generalizability of our conclusions regarding ER measurements in adolescents, as the focus is primarily on younger age groups. Second, the review excluded questionnaire-based methods to enhance readability, meaning that our analysis of psychometric properties is confined to behavioral observation and physiological measurement methods, which may omit relevant insights from self-report instruments. Third, the available data on psychometric properties were limited to a subset of studies, as a considerable proportion of studies did not report any psychometric information.
elements.reason: The discussion section explicitly states multiple limitations of the included evidence (age-range restriction, exclusion of questionnaire methods, incomplete psychometric reporting, limited diversity and narrow clinical scope), satisfying the requirement to discuss limitations.
